claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: private and protected are only enforced during type checking. … private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking. … these fields are soft private
claim_checks.note: The handbook covers type-check-only enforcement and runtime lookup for both modifiers, and bracket access for private; the co-cited probe-01 tests bracket access to a protected member (tsc 5.9.3 exit 0, same on tsc7 per harness.json), so the two citations together cover the claim.

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks will degrade performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. … Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: First sentence is supported. The second raises the handbook's 'could affect' to 'will degrade' (a hedge written as 'will'). It also narrows the note: the handbook's sentence covers all hard-privacy mechanisms (closures, WeakMaps, or private fields), including native #, not only the downlevelled WeakMaps.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` copies them like public fields.
claim_checks.page_says: For this reason, structuredClone() does not clone private elements, and Object.freeze() and Object.seal() have no effect on private elements.
claim_checks.note: The first two sentences match MDN ('they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method'). The structuredClone clause inverts MDN. probe-02 cannot support it: JSON.stringify never shows # fields, so its expected '{}' is printed whether or not anything was copied, and that output is itself consistent with MDN.

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: a TypeError is thrown, instead of returning undefined as normal properties do. … This will return true if the private field or method exists, and false otherwise.
claim_checks.note: MDN's example error reads 'Cannot read private member #x from an object whose class did not declare it'; the in-check returns true or false for an object.

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.4 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: The first issue has been fixed in V8 v9.7 … Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call for class field initializations.
claim_checks.note: The page gives v9.7, not 9.4 (the doc's own front matter says V8 ≥ 9.7). The claim also drops the page's condition that the new IC is used 'when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough', falling back to a runtime call otherwise.

claim_checks.claim: A `#` name cannot be a parameter property (row: An injected collaborator (port, clock, logger) → `private readonly x` constructor parameter).
claim_checks.page_says: That this is not possible is a bit surprising because it increases the friction of refactoring
claim_checks.note: The cited issue (a 2020 feature request) supports the statement, but it is Rank 6 cited in a role 3 section: a KB-15 breach, recorded under violations. The uncited Rank 1 handbook supports it too: parameter properties 'are created by prefixing a constructor argument with one of the visibility modifiers public, private, protected, or readonly'.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements cannot be proxied (row: Object wrapped in a `Proxy` → `#` access does not go through the proxy).
claim_checks.page_says: While private elements are accessed with the familiar dot notation, they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.

claim_checks.claim: TypeScript downlevels it (row: Target ES2021 or lower → `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups).
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: Working around it with `--experimental-transform-types`: runs on Node 24.22 with an `ExperimentalWarning` (re-tested 2026-11-03); the flag is removed in Node 26.0.0. So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor.
claim_checks.note: The removal in 26.0.0 is supported. The Node 24.22 behaviour (runs, emits ExperimentalWarning) is not in the saved page, which is the v26.13.1 documentation; searched 'ExperimentalWarning', 'warning', 'transform-types'. The re-test has no probe or other artifact in the input.

claim_checks.claim: Type stripping itself: Stable (stability 2) since Node 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; Node ignores `tsconfig.json` and needs `.ts` extensions in relative imports. Node only deletes types.
claim_checks.page_says: | v24.3.0, v22.18.0 | Type stripping no longer emits an experimental warning.
claim_checks.note: Stability, the 24.12.0/25.2.0 versions, tsconfig.json being ignored, mandatory file extensions in imports and 'only removing inline types' are all supported. 'No warning' drops the page's qualifier 'experimental'.

claim_checks.claim: In Node 24.22.1, `Object.getOwnPropertyNames()` never lists a `#` field.
claim_checks.page_says: n/a: cites only the local artifact probes/probe-03.js
claim_checks.note: Not checkable against saved web text, but the cited probe cannot fail: the empty catch swallows every error and console.log('not listed') runs unconditionally, and the check names.length > 5 never looks for '#x'. Its harness 'pass' is no evidence. MDN [^2] (not cited here) would support the statement: private elements cannot be 'interacted with using any Object method'.

conflicts.topic: Runtime cost of native # fields. The Summary and Takeaways say reading and creating # fields costs the same as public fields (cost 'nil'), resting on the unarchived Worked example measurement. The Rank 1 handbook says hard-privacy mechanisms including private fields 'could affect performance', and the Rank 4 V8 blog limits the fast path to predictable initialization patterns. These hedge rather than contradict the measurement, so no arbitration is required. But the doc hides the handbook caveat by attributing it to WeakMaps only (C3), and role 6 does not mention it.
conflicts.loser: Worked example measurement, rank local (no artifact)

violations.evidence: C3: item 3 says the handbook notes runtime privacy checks 'will degrade performance'; the handbook says they 'could affect performance', and it says this of closures, WeakMaps and private fields alike, not only the downlevelled WeakMaps.

C4: item 4 says 'structuredClone() copies them like public fields'; MDN [^2] says 'structuredClone() does not clone private elements'. The co-cited probe-02 cannot tell the cases apart, since JSON.stringify prints '{}' for an object whose only field is private whether or not it was cloned.

C6: item 6 dates the inline-cache fix to V8 9.4; the V8 blog [^3] says 'The first issue has been fixed in V8 v9.7' and 'Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call'. The doc's own applies-to says V8 ≥ 9.7.

The 'Where each form fits' row 'An injected collaborator' cites ✅[^5], github.com/microsoft/TypeScript/issues/36282 (tier A, Rank 6, rule github.com/*/*/issues/), in a role 3 section that allows ranks 1–4.

C12: the ✅[^probe-03] mark rests on a probe that passes for any outcome. probes/probe-03.js wraps the check in try { … } catch {} and then prints 'not listed' unconditionally, and its only test (names.length > 5) never checks for '#x'. The ✅ therefore has no evidence behind it and counts as an uncited core ✅.
[^6] (github.com/tc39/proposal-class-fields, 'Backs: How it works 2') is never cited in the body; How it works item 2 cites only [^1].

C10: the Node 24.22 'runs with an ExperimentalWarning' part of the --experimental-transform-types row is not in the cited Node docs (saved page is v26.13.1), and the re-test it mentions has no artifact.
C11: 'no warning since 24.3.0' drops the qualifier; the page says type stripping 'no longer emits an experimental warning' (v24.3.0, v22.18.0).

The status says 'Verified: 10 claims (✅) · Unverified: 0 claims (⚠️)'. The body has 12 ✅-closed claims (14 marks), and several factual statements carry neither mark: the Summary's performance sentence, every Worked example number, and the Edge cases row on ERR_UNSUPPORTED_TYPESCRIPT_SYNTAX / TS1294 ('Reproduced on Node 24.22').

The run gives outputs (timings, Object.keys results) but not the benchmark program or any artifact, so the inputs cannot be reproduced. The doc also has no role 2 or role 5 section, and How it works mixes invariants and a decision table under a mechanism heading.
